newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair promises Britain a fresh start.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair promises Britain a fresh start.

text.p: Opposition Labour party leader Tony Blair on Thursday promised Britain a fresh start with different priorities and different values if he wins the May 1 election.

In an interview with BBC radio ahead of the publication of the party's election manifesto, he said he would keep Britain's options open on joining a single European currency and that all of his party's spending proposals would be properly costed.
"I do not promise you that I can wave a magic wand, create extra money overnight and the whole of the world's problems are put to right," he said.

"What I can promise you is that there will be a fresh start with different priorities, different values and bit by bit we will rebuild the education system, the health service and the welfare state in this country.
Blair said Labour would have to keep to tough spending limits but that his government would do things differently. His main priorities would be education and getting young people back to work.
"There are no promises that we have made that aren't funded," he said.
Blair, who at 43 will be the youngest prime minister this century if he ousts the Conservatives after 18 years in power, said he was convinced Britons were tired of the government's broken promises.
The latest opinion poll in The Times newspaper, which put Labour at 55 percent, far ahead of the Conservatives who trailed at 28 percent, seemed to confirm his belief.
Blair said the Conservative's manifesto released on Wednesday included a load of promises, but that he would not make promises he could not keep.
In a personal "contract" with Britain, released on Wednesday, the Labour leader promises he will not raise income tax rates and will provide stable non-inflationary growth.

He says education will be his government's "Number One priority", and spending on it will rise. He also vows to use a windfall tax on surplus profits of water, gas, electricity and other firms privatised by the Conservatives to take 250,000 people out of the dole queues.

Other pledges include more money for National Health Service patient care, the safeguarding of Britain's environment, a cleanup of politics following a bout of sleaze and to "give Britain the leadership in Europe which Britain and Europe need."
"We want a tax system that encourages work," Blair said. "Our priority in the tax system is to reduce the starting rate of tax."

The 10-point programme, crafted to ensure that the Conservatives cannot attack Labour for profligate spending plans, contains no new promises compared with Blair's keynote speech to last October's annual party conference.
